book: 255 - The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute
essays: 1. How to De-Nazify Nietzsche’s Philosophical Anthropology
2. Misinterpretation as the Author’s Responsibility (Nietzsche’s fascism, for instance)
6. Nietzsche contra Wagner on the Jews
7. Between the Cross and the Swastika A Nietzschean Perspective
9. A Question of Responsibility Nietzsche with Hölderlin at War, 1914 –1946
10. The Elisabeth Legend The Cleansing of Nietzsche and the Sullying of His Sister
12. Nietzsche and the Fascist Dimension The Case of Ernst Jünger
13. A Godfather Too Nazism as a Nietzschean “Experiment”
14. Critique as Apologetics Nolte’s Interpretation of Nietzsche
samples: Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.

Golomb argues the Nazi reading of the will to power as military conquest confuses Nietzsche's Macht (sublimated spiritual power) with Kraft (brute force) and Gewalt (violence), showing through Human, All Too Human and Daybreak that self-overcoming and creative sublimation, not domination, define the Übermensch. He builds a typology of 'positive' versus 'negative' power in which the anti-Semite figures as the vengeful, ressentiment-driven 'slave,' and insists Nietzsche's morality is not naturalistic—power must be transfigured by self-education—so his anthropology stands beyond the eugenic and racial distinctions central to Nazi ideology, even in the misused 'blond beast' passage.

Berel Lang asks whether an author is responsible for being misinterpreted, defining a 'Fascist Minimum' (priority of the state over the individual, plus natural inequality asserted through war) and testing Nietzsche against it. He finds Nietzsche flatly rejects the first condition—his 'coldest of all cold monsters' attacks on the state and nationalism—and accepts the second only with heavy qualification. Lang locates Nietzsche's partial culpability in a 'Fallacy of Composition' by which readers like Bäumler transposed individual will to power onto the collective state, arguing that Nietzsche, foreseeing this abuse, chose not to 'build a fence' around his meaning and so bears responsibility 'up to a point.'

Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.

Nehamas puts 'Hitler' in scare-quotes to pose an abstract problem—does Nietzsche's ideal of nobility permit the evil hero?—rooting it in the Greek notion of aretê and Plato's Republic. He argues Nietzsche's own doctrine that 'there is no doer behind the deed' (Genealogy I:13) collapses the split between noble soul and noble action, so that deeds confer status; using the case of the police torturing a random woman and the fortuitousness of the Jews' extermination, he contends that when what separates us from victims is mere accident we are their peers, and Nietzsche needs the very doer/deed distinction he attacks in order to reject morality absolutely, so his refusal to condemn the evil hero can be refuted on Nietzschean grounds.

Brinker surveys Duffy-Mittelman, Santaniello, and Yovel to argue that reading Nietzsche as simply pro-Jewish oversimplifies a genuine ambivalence toward the 'Jewish race' running through all periods of Jewish history. He shows that in The Antichrist Nietzsche separates ressentiment from decadence: Jesus is the 'most perfect decadent' incapable of hatred, while Paul and the priests embody ressentiment, and the Jews, being too strong to be decadent, cunningly poison their conquerors with a faith they do not share—an old anti-Semitic stereotype transplanted into new soil. Brinker concludes this ambivalence, plus Nietzsche's post-Zarathustra equation of equality, democracy, and socialism with slave-morality decadence, is exactly what let the Nazis manipulate him.

book: 256 - Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life
essays: 2. To Eat or Not to Eat
4. How Anthony Bourdain United the Local and the Universal
5. Friendship, Fun, Freedom, Food, and the Future
6. Authenticity in a World of Bullshido
8. Why Do We Care Who Bourdain Really Was
11. The One Truly Serious Philosophical Problem
15. The Subtle Persuasion of Culinary Adventure Programs
18. The Journey May Also Save Us
samples: This editor's introduction frames Bourdain as a modern philosopher by playing a variation on his 'Last Meal' game and choosing Bourdain as the ideal dinner companion. It argues that Bourdain's professed humility about how little he knows ('realizing how small I am, and unwise') echoes Socratic ignorance and the love of wisdom, and previews the volume's questions about happiness, authenticity, taste, and freedom.

Shaffer uses Brillat-Savarin's distinction between direct and reflective taste and Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' to argue gastronomic expertise is only the acquired ability to describe tastes richly, not a superior sense. He then casts Bourdain as a culinary Socrates who, like the freed prisoner in Plato's allegory of the cave, returns to lead provincial eaters out of the darkness of narrow experience toward cultural tolerance.

Barta and Miranda read Bourdain's 'good eating is all about risk' credo through Bentham's cost-benefit hedonic calculus, sorting risk/reward into Ascetic, Epicurean, Cyrenaic, and Utilitarian quadrants. They classify Bourdain's fugu-eating and drunk cliff-driving as failed calculations, his comfort-food returns as Epicurean, and his gluttonous adventures (French Laundry, Russian vodka) as Cyrenaic high-risk/high-reward living.

Calef asks how Bourdain could find disgusting foods (cobra heart, blood soup, warthog anus) delicious, using Korsmeyer's taxonomy of disgust and the 'paradox of aversion.' He argues their appeal comes from Aristotelian learning-through-representation, Burke's and Bullough's sublime experienced at psychical distance, and Kristeva's 'abject' — foods that remind us of death and mortality let Bourdain transcend and disarm it by eating them appreciatively.

Barta and Miranda contrast Kant's 'universally communicable' taste with Bourdieu's view that taste is a social construct shaped by field, habitus, and cultural capital that reinforces class distinctions. Using Bourdain's episodes (Portuguese bacalao, New York hot dogs, the French Laundry), they argue he synthesizes both: acknowledging taste's locality while democratizing it as a cosmopolitan 'citizen of the world' in the tradition of Diogenes and Kant's perpetual peace.

Le Gall and Taliaferro read Bourdain's Libya and Iran episodes of Parts Unknown through Pierre Hadot's 'philosophy as a way of life,' arguing that Gaddafi and Khomeini were failed Platonic philosopher-kings. They interpret ordinary Libyans and Iranians eating Uncle Kentucky chicken, playing pinball, or hosting feasts as popular 'spiritual exercises' — tatonnement — showing how the personal becomes political and how friendship, fun, freedom, and food nourish the Socratic care of the soul.

book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today
essays: The Talking Cure for Our Culture
“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”
The Role of Matter Biology or Function
Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy
samples: Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.

Arp uses cartoon Johnnie Cochran's 'Chewbacca Defense' from 'Chef Aid' to teach basic logic: the structure of arguments (premises and conclusion), premise/conclusion indicators, and the difference between deductive validity and inductive strength, illustrated with Cartman's tooth-fairy and Towelie arguments. The Chewbacca Defense is a red-herring fallacy, and other episodes illustrate hasty generalization, slippery slope, false dilemma, appeal to inappropriate authority, and ad hominem. Arp argues South Park deliberately violates logical principles to expose the absurdity and real harm of bad reasoning.

Johnson uses Stephen Colbert's coinages to refute relativism and gut-thinking. 'My Truth' represents individual relativism and 'Wikiality' cultural relativism, both of which Johnson rejects via the correspondence theory of truth and counterexamples like slavery and Nazi Germany. 'Truthiness' is intuitionism, which Johnson attacks using Locke's critique of 'enthusiasts' who reason in a circle, and he argues that appeals to 'a right to my opinion' reveal indifference to truth. Following Socrates, he concludes we should defend beliefs with argument and admit ignorance rather than trust the gut.

Jacoby uses Stan Marsh as the embodiment of W. K. Clifford's ethics of belief, that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence. Stan debunks TV psychic John Edward, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the one making extraordinary claims. Jacoby distinguishes evidential from prudential reasons, presents and criticizes Pascal's Wager (using 'Cartmanland' and the problem of undeserved suffering), and argues via Clifford that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken the mind and, as Stan tells Edward, slow 'the progress of all mankind.'

Lawrence uses The Matrix to raise Cartesian skepticism: Neo's deception dramatizes Descartes's dream argument and evil demon, the computer-run Matrix being a technological version of the demon. He argues even Morpheus cannot be certain he has truly awakened ('the Matrix within the Matrix'), so the only certainty is Descartes's cogito. Drawing on Russell's 'Appearance and Reality,' he then argues that even setting aside Matrix scenarios, naive realism fails, since a chair's color, texture, solidity and shape are all perception-relative, leaving the external world's nature deeply uncertain.

Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.

book: 259 - Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons
essays: Part Five D Is for Destiny
None of It Matters Anyway, Then, Does It
If Not on the Island of Ethical Subjectivism, Then Where
Keep the Needle on the Record
samples: This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.

Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.

William J. Devlin applies David Lewis's distinction between external time and the traveler's personal time to Lost's season 5-6 time jumps, showing how Faraday's eternalist 'whatever happened, happened' (Chang's unbreakable rules) contrasts with the branching-universe model that Faraday later embraces with 'we're the variables.' Lewis's account resolves specific puzzles: why baby Miles and adult Miles can coexist without violating the indiscernibility of identicals, whether Faraday could kill his mother Eloise (the grandfather paradox), and the uncaused causal loop of the compass Locke and Richard pass between 1954 and 2007.

Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'

Deborah R. Barnbaum reads season 6's flash-sideways as a set of counterfactual conditionals ('if Sawyer weren't a con man, then he would have been a cop') and uses David Lewis's possible-worlds semantics and his ordered similarity priorities to judge which are plausible. She argues Sawyer-as-cop is a 'closest world' change of one fact while Jack-and-Juliet-with-a-son changes too much to be true, and she pairs this with Rawls's veil of ignorance and A Theory of Justice as a parallel counterfactual thought experiment governing how the castaways should ration scarce water and medicine.

Charles Taliaferro and Dan Kastrul argue, following Aristotle's dispositional account of character, that who the castaways are is a matter of what they would do under different conditions, illustrated by Mr. Eko's circumstance-driven violence and Ben Linus's shifting good-guy/bad-guy conduct. They deploy Plato's Myth of Gyges (the ring of invisibility) to test whether characters like Sun would act justly only when watched, and, against a completely reversed morality ('an island where skinning babies is good'), they argue via Chesterton that some overriding values are non-relative, so the show never fully reverses good and evil even amid its mysteries.

samples: Gerald Erion reads The Daily Show through Neil Postman's Amusing Ourselves to Death, arguing that Stewart's opening headline mockery of hurricane 'reporters in canoes,' 'Senior Correspondents,' and graphics packages like 'Mess O'Potamia' targets not the day's events but television's own entertainment bias, which renders even serious news trivial. He treats Stewart's Crossfire plea to 'stop hurting America,' the Jim Cramer 'Brawl Street' interview, and the Rally to Restore Sanity's '24-hour politico pundit perpetual panic conflictinator' as Postman-style critiques that a medium built to amuse cannot carry rational public discourse.

Michael Gettings asks how a self-described 'fake news' show informs viewers, and answers with the philosophical puzzle of how fiction conveys truth. He classifies Daily Show reports as non-deceptive pretense (Stewart's 'hilarious make-'em-ups' like Santorum's safe word) rather than lies, and shows how hyperbole (Samantha Bee on North Korean soldiers), the straight-man/correspondent roles, and graphics cue the audience to what is real. He argues the show's fictions carry both particular truths (the Kyl Planned Parenthood '90%' lie) and general truths about government and cable news, contrasting its news-anchored humor with The Onion's stereotype-driven invention.

Rachael Sotos casts The Daily Show as the ethos of a 'Fifth Estate' that watches the failing Fourth, invoking Hannah Arendt's distinction between the actor and the spectator to defend Stewart's insistence that he is a comedian, not an activist or journalist: it is precisely by withdrawing from action that the bard-spectator gives events meaning. She traces Stewart and Colbert's satirical, pseudonymous lineage to Ben Franklin (Silence Dogood, Polly Baker) and Juvenalian/Horatian satire, arguing the Super PAC saga and the Rally to Restore Sanity's 'moment of sincerity' function like the parabasis of Aristophanic Old Comedy.

Greg Littmann defends political mockery as an ancient tradition (Aristophanes, Juvenal, Twain) but warns, using J.S. Mill's On Liberty, that if viewers let The Daily Show's jokes substitute for reasoned judgment the effect is like censorship, silencing ideas that must be heard to be understood. He cites Mill's arguments against silencing discussion and Plato's Meno on shackling true opinion with reasons, arguing that Stewart's virtue over Limbaugh is that he bills himself as comedy ('the show that leads into me is puppets making crank phone calls') and never presents mockery as a replacement for informed citizenship.

Kellie Bean reads Colbert and Stewart through Jean Baudrillard's simulacra and the hyperreal, arguing that mainstream news has become an image unmoored from reality. Colbert is a 'walking talking simulacrum' who out-O'Reillys O'Reilly (the portrait-within-a-portrait, 'The Word' segments like 'Gateway Hug'), enacting news as pure sign; Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal to expose the real, parsing Obama's convention rhetoric and Laura Ingraham's platform dodge. The 'Best F#@king News Team Ever' slogan lays bare the empty hyperbole of 'Fair and Balanced,' re-anchoring the audience to meaning.

Terrance MacMullan argues Stewart is America's most effective public intellectual, reviving the engaged tradition of Emerson, William James, Dewey, and Du Bois against the isolation Rorty diagnosed in academics. Using Cornel West's account of pragmatism as 'explaining America to itself,' he reads segments like 'Victory Lapse,' the Karl Rove 'what honor' bit, and 'Gitmo's World' as pragmatist cultural criticism, and casts Stewart's 'Worst Responders' campaign for the 9/11 Zadroga Bill and his amicable debates with conservatives as embodying Dewey's democracy as a shared 'working faith' in people.

essays: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing
samples: Hooke and Rivera's editors' introduction argues that The Twilight Zone dramatizes the Nietzschean disappointment of the epigraph from Twilight of the Idols—that we seek great human beings and find only 'the apes of their ideal.' They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnated Socrates, a gadfly whose episodes ('Time Enough at Last,' 'The Hunt,' the eternal-youth trade-in) stage the gap between our ideals of love, justice, and truth and the treacherous, self-deluding creatures we actually are, so that viewers laugh at absurd twist endings because we are the species most deserving to be laughed at.

Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.

Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of surrealist philosophy (Breton, Dalí) that provokes the Freudian 'uncanny.' He traces a line from Descartes—whose cogito and 'clear and distinct' rational mind produced the mind–body problem that lets surrealists destabilize waking reality—through psychoanalysis to Breton's 'point' where real and imagined cease to be contradictions. Episodes like 'A World of His Own' (automatic writing), 'The Mirror' (Dalí's paranoiac-critical method), 'Shadow Play,' 'The Shelter,' and 'The Lonely' unleash the imagination unbound by reason and provoke the uncanny in viewers.

Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a meditation on our ambivalent dependence on technology and other people. Henry Bemis experiences the bank, his marriage, and finally the post-nuclear wasteland as successive 'cages' where time belongs to others; his misanthropic wish for a timeless world to himself is granted only for his glasses to shatter, revealing his short-sighted fantasy of exempting himself from the technological system on which even his vision depends. Pichanick concludes the episode demands not another pair of glasses but a philosophical clarity about our limits and interdependence.

Hooke, drawing on Levinas and his translator Alphonso Lingis, treats the face as the site where trust in a stranger is risked. The Twilight Zone weaponizes our trust in familiar (actors') faces: death wears Robert Redford's face in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Satan is the avuncular Pip in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the Kanamits' gentle faces mask a cookbook in 'To Serve Man.' He invokes the Turing test for Corry and Alicia's love in 'The Lonely,' and finds the most truthful face of love in 'The Trade-Ins,' where the aged couple cannot bear each other's altered faces after rejuvenation.

Klayman analyzes whether James Corry's love for the robot Alicia in 'The Lonely' is true love, using C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their three qualities (gift-, need-, appreciative-love), plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim to define 'truly loving' by its practical effects. He argues true love falls within Eros and requires a reciprocating individual, invoking Peter Singer's speciesism to reject a human-only requirement; concluding Corry showed only appreciative-love (not gift- or need-love) and that his bond was really companionship—Corry became fictional (Walton) to have something to believe in.

book: 262 - Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!
essays: Oh, the Places You’ll Go! The Examined, Happy Life
My Troubles Are Going to Have Troubles with Me Schopenhauer, Pessimism, and Nietzsche
Gertrude McFuzz Should’ve Read Marx, or Sneetches of the World Unite
Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation
Neither Here, nor There, nor Anywhere
On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet
From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere
What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics
Horton Hears You, Too! Seuss and Kant on Respecting Persons
Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax
The Grinch’s Change of Heart Whodunit
Thidwick the Big-Hearted Bearer of Property Rights
Rebellion in Sala-ma-Sond The Social Contract and a Turtle Named Mack
Whose Egg Is It, Really Property Rights and Distributive Justice
It’s Not Personal . . . It’s Just Bizzyneuss Business Ethics, the Company, and Its Stakeholders
Speaking for Business, Speaking for Trees Business and Environment in The Lorax
samples: Benjamin Rider reads Oh, the Places You'll Go! through Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living. He argues the Sneetches' star-obsession, Yertle's tower, Gertrude McFuzz's feathers, and the Once-ler's 'biggering' are the false, unexamined beliefs about wealth and status that Socrates said wreck the soul, while Bartholomew Cubbins and Horton model the wise, courageous endurance Socrates seeks but fails to define with the generals Laches and Nicias in Plato's Laches. The 'Waiting Place' becomes the life of someone who never questions what really makes him happy, and Seuss's call to use 'the brains in your head' echoes Socrates' insistence in the Crito and Phaedo on living by rational reflection.

Jacob Held pits Schopenhauer's pessimism against Nietzschean affirmation using I Had Trouble in Getting to Solla Sollew. He reads Schopenhauer's will-to-life and 'pendulum between pain and boredom' into Seuss's endlessly striving characters, and treats the mirage-towns Solla Sollew and Boola Boo Ball as proof there is no escape from suffering. The protagonist's final line, 'I've bought a big bat... now my troubles are going to have troubles with me,' becomes Nietzsche's yes-saying: instead of the ascetic renunciation Schopenhauer prescribes, Seuss's child-hero affirms life, redeeming its accidents the way Nietzsche's eternal-recurrence thought experiment and 'become a child' passage in Zarathustra demand.

Jacob Held uses the Once-ler, Pontoffel Pock, the Sneetches, and Gertrude McFuzz to explain Marx's theory of alienation. The Once-ler is the capitalist owning the means of Thneed production; Pontoffel Pock's dull pickle-works job shows labor severed from the worker's essence as a free, conscious producer (an idea Held traces to Hegel on self-expression through work). The Sneetches buying stars from Sylvester McMonkey McBean and Gertrude popping pill-berries dramatize how alienated people chase belonging through consumption, which Held elaborates via Fromm's 'having vs being' and Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry, concluding the fault lies not in the characters but in a society that denies self-realization through labor.

Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.

Randall Auxier reads Green Eggs and Ham as a primer in Peircean pragmatism. The contrarian 'C' illustrates how thinking only begins when a problem interrupts action, and Peirce's distinction between 'genuine doubt' and settled belief-as-habit explains why C clings to 'I do not like them' without ever trying them. Auxier runs C's stubbornness through Peirce's four methods of fixing belief (Authority, A Priori, Tenacity, Science), arguing C relies on tenacity, and likens Sam-I-Am to Saint Monica pestering Augustine into genuine doubt, so that even after C eats the eggs he only knows they settled belief in one context.

Ron Novy uses Marco's faith that unseen fish swim in McElligot's Pool to survey theories of knowledge as justified true belief. The farmer's empiricism and Marco's inference from a book frame a tour through Descartes's evil-genius doubt and skepticism, Locke's primary/secondary qualities (indirect realism), Berkeley's idealism ('to be is to be perceived'), and rationalist a priori knowledge, before turning to feminist epistemology (Schott, Kant's 'intuitions without concepts are blind,' Nietzsche on perspectival seeing) and Quine's naturalized epistemology to argue knowers are situated and the pool may indeed be 'bigger than you or I know.'

essays: There Is No God in Desperation
Propaganda and Pedagogy for Apt Pupils
The Shining ’s Overlook Hotel as Heterotopia
Stephen King and the Art of Horror
What Happens to the Present When It Becomes the Past
Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone
samples: Jacob Held defends the philosophy-and-popular-culture project against snobbery and argues that King's horror is genuine philosophy because it forces readers to confront finitude, meaning, and their deepest values. He reads King's own account of 'existential horror' through Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian pairing, casting the horror tale as a Dionysian crack in an Apollonian order that ends by restoring equilibrium, and frames doing this fun, relatable work as its own eudaimonia poised between nihilism and Aristotelian flourishing. Using Lovecraft's Cthulhu and King's Desperation/The Regulators (Tak), he claims horror shakes us into reaffirming the values that orient us and so bridges abstract academic philosophy and lived experience.

Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.

Kellye Byal reads Carrie White through Beauvoir's The Second Sex, treating Carrie's first menstruation, her mother Margaret's ascetic 'Mystic' piety, and Miss Collins/Sue Snell's push toward makeup and the prom as two imposed versions of 'feminine destiny.' Carrie is caught between rejecting femininity (becoming an outcast/monster) and assuming it (surrendering her subjectivity to immanence and the male gaze), so her telekinesis becomes an externalized act of authentic, radically free agency against both scripts. Byal argues her tragic death indicts a failed community of women who never posit themselves as Subjects, illustrating Beauvoir's claim that female subjectivity needs a solidarity of others in which to thrive.

Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.

Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.

Matthew Butkus reads Roland Deschain of The Dark Tower as a parallel to Rama of the Ramayana and Arjuna of the Bhagavad Gita, mapping his cyclical existence onto the Hindu concepts of karma (his coupling with the demon spawning Mordred, letting Jake fall), dharma (the gunslinger's duty to protect the Beams as an avatar restoring cosmic order), samskara (character shaped by all past lives) and samsara (the death-rebirth cycle the Horn of Eld may or may not break). Like Krishna instructing the reluctant Arjuna, the text tells Roland he must 'stand and be true' regardless of misgivings; Butkus concludes the moral for readers is not violence but fulfilling one's own svadharma—to stand and be true in one's own station.

Marinucci's editorial introduction surveys the volume, framing Austen's six novels as a body of work with philosophical value across love/marriage, morality/virtue, wealth/class, concepts, and zombie mashups. It previews each contributor's thesis: Bufacchi reading Anne Elliot and the Bennets through Fricker's epistemic injustice, Dougherty aligning Austen's ideal marriage with Aristotelian complete friendship, Lindenmuth pairing Austen with Nietzsche on marital happiness, and Bane's Marxist reading of the 1940 Pride and Prejudice film. It argues Austen is an 'accidental philosopher' whose insight into social relations, especially women's vulnerability, carries philosophical weight.

Bufacchi applies Fricker's testimonial and hermeneutical epistemic injustice to Austen's heroines, arguing women like Anne Elliot ('only Anne,' her word carrying no weight) and Elizabeth Bennet are denied credibility as knowers, while Mr. Collins's certainty that a woman's 'no' means 'yes' shows men's epistemic arrogance. He layers in Young's structural injustice to explain the Bennet women's economic vulnerability under entailment, then extends Fricker with his own 'Perpetuating Force of Epistemic Injustice': Emma Woodhouse, herself a victim, becomes a perpetrator by silencing Harriet Smith's love for the farmer Robert Martin, showing how the oppressed reproduce the injustice on those below them.

Winkle reads Sense and Sensibility as steering a 'middle road' between cold rational calculation and sentimental self-indulgence, and casts Austen as proto-feminist. She uses Wollstonecraft's Vindication to explain why Austen's silly wives (Mrs. Bennet, Lucy Steele) are products of a deficient female education that trains women to please rather than reason. She then reads Elinor Dashwood's measured love for Edward, and Marianne's near-fatal collapse over Willoughby, through bell hooks's claim that 'falling in love' surrenders agency, arguing Elinor chooses love as an act of will while Marianne must learn sense before finding lasting love with Colonel Brandon.

Gibson argues Austen's novels are propelled by dialectical forces (signaled by titles like Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility) that are reconciled through the marriage bond, invoking the Platonic origin of dialectic and drawing on Harold Bloom's reading of Darcy and Elizabeth as sharing a common will. Love functions as the transcendent principle that resolves opposition, but Gibson stresses (citing Derrida on the gift) that in Austen love never fully escapes the economic and social 'prisons' of marriage: Charlotte Lucas's loveless match, Fanny Price's poverty, and Anne Elliot's coerced broken engagement all show love succeeding only alongside wealth and status.

Lindenmuth pairs Austen with Nietzsche on what makes a happy marriage, reading Pride and Prejudice's clashes over Lizzy's refusals of Mr. Collins and Darcy, and Lady Catherine's and Sir Thomas Bertram's aristocratic insistence that superiors should choose for inferiors. He uses Nietzsche's 'philosophizing with a hammer' to cast Austen as smashing the dead traditions of entailment and arranged marriage, and Nietzsche's aphorisms (a good marriage rests on a talent for friendship and good conversation; sensuality makes love grow too fast) to judge the couples, concluding Austen holds an Aristotelian, objective view of happiness as a reward for getting life right rather than mere desire-satisfaction.

Dougherty argues Austen's ideal marriage mirrors Aristotle's complete friendship, where the friend is loved for who they are and becomes a 'second self.' She sorts Austen's relationships into Aristotle's three kinds: utility (Emma and Mrs. Elton, Charlotte and Mr. Collins), pleasure (Lydia and Wickham, the fading Emma-Harriet bond), and complete friendship grounded in mutual good character (Jane and Bingley, Elizabeth and Darcy, Emma and Knightley). Central is the 'second self' as mirror: Darcy's letter and Knightley's rebukes let Elizabeth and Emma see themselves ('Till this moment I never knew myself'), so marriage-as-friendship improves self-knowledge and virtue and must not be left to chance as Charlotte urges.

samples: Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.

Jonathan Bennett reads the chapter 16 raft episode as a clash between 'bad morality' and sympathy: Huck's conscience (slave-owning principles telling him to return Jim to Miss Watson) supplies all the reasons, while his sympathy for Jim is a bare, reasonless feeling that wins by weakness of will, so Huck does right while believing he does wrong. He contrasts Huck with Himmler, whose bad morality overrode his surviving sympathy, and Jonathan Edwards, whose Calvinist approval of eternal damnation left no sympathy to conflict. The lesson is that principles should be kept open to revision under pressure from sympathy, since one cannot declare one's own morality bad but should stay open to correction.

Alan Goldman argues against Bennett and against Arpaly and Schroeder that Huck is not weak-willed or irrational: his sympathy for Jim is an intentional emotion containing implicit judgments and awareness of the genuine moral reasons to help Jim, so Huck acts on his strongest reasons and is courageous rather than akratic. Because Huck is rational yet not motivated by his explicit (corrupt) moral judgments, and his real motivation comes only through emotional attachment, Goldman concludes against Kant that moral motivation is not rationally required. He uses Huck's failure to extend concern to other slaves, and analogies to meat-eaters and arbitrary aesthetic taste, to show moral inconsistency is not practical irrationality.

Robert Fudge uses Adam Smith to reinterpret Huck's conscience and praiseworthiness. Against Bennett (conscience as accepted principles) and Arpaly-Schroeder (inverse akrasia via a whole-self theory), Fudge argues, following Smith, that conscience is the sentiment-based judgment of the 'man within the breast,' the impartial spectator, and that propriety rests on sympathetic 'feeling with' others rather than abstract principle. Huck's sympathy for Jim in the chapter 16 raft scene is a reason-bearing emotion, so he is not acting akratically or against his true conscience; instead he is growing morally, molding his conscience toward the loyalty and friendship that already constitute his core self.

Michael Lyons defends the 'pedestal' of moral principles against Bennett's chapter 16 reading. He accepts that sympathy rightly saved Jim and that Edwards's principled cruelty and Himmler's suppressed sympathy show principles must be revisable, but rejects the stronger claim that sympathy should override conduct while leaving conflicting principles intact. Reconstructing Bennett's argument into 'stronger' and 'adjusted' versions, Lyons argues principles remain the best primary guide once corrected by sympathy, and that Twain shows Huck retaining a natural, humanity-grounded morality even after rejecting society's 'deformed conscience.' He prizes incorruptibility, sticking to correct principles, as the mark of the highest heroism Huck could aspire to.

Kristina Gehrman argues that reading Huck as a moral hero who overcomes racism is Twain's ironic trap. Using Arne Naess's idea of identification, Aristotle on habituation of character, and Iris Murdoch's 'just and loving attention,' she gives a developmentally attuned reading of Huck as a traumatized, morally immature, still-racist child whose regard for Jim never generalizes ('I knowed he was white inside'). Twain lures his white readers into identifying with Huck's supposed triumph, then exposes their own stunted moral growth about race; Jim is the only mature adult yet is barred from identification by the novel's racist caricature. The novel's greatness is Socratic and gadfly-like rather than triumphant.
